exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with sickle cell disease presents with sudden severe pain and Hb 6 g/dL – what immediate steps and why? — Assess airway, give analgesia, hydrate, order CBC and retic, consider transfusion if unstable; avoid NSAIDs if renal risk.

A 45‑year‑old man with chronic cough, weight loss, Hb 9 g/dL, MCV 78 fL – which investigation distinguishes TB‑related anaemia from iron deficiency? — Perform sputum GeneXpert and ferritin; low ferritin points to iron deficiency, normal/high ferritin with TB suggests anaemia of chronic disease.

A child from a malaria‑endemic area has pallor, Hb 8 g/dL, and a peripheral smear shows parasites – what is the primary management and what red flag prompts urgent referral? — Start ACT per protocol; if Hb <5 g/dL or signs of cardiac failure, arrange urgent transfusion.

A pregnant woman in her second trimester has Hb 10 g/dL, MCV 85 fL, normal ferritin – what is the likely cause and how to treat? — Likely anaemia of chronic disease or physiologic dilution; monitor, give folic acid, treat any infection; iron not indicated.

A patient on antiretroviral therapy presents with macrocytic anaemia – which drug is most likely responsible and what alternative should be considered? — Zidovudine causes macrocytosis; switch to tenofovir‑based regimen if renal function permits.

A 60‑year‑old man with chronic kidney disease has Hb 9 g/dL, normal iron studies – why might erythropoietin be indicated and what monitoring is required? — CKD reduces erythropoietin; start ESA after ruling out iron deficiency; monitor Hb weekly to avoid overshoot.

A patient with severe anaemia and jaundice – how do you differentiate haemolysis from hepatic failure? — Check retic count (high in haemolysis), LDH, haptoglobin; bilirubin predominately indirect in haemolysis, direct in liver disease.
ai.title: Approach to Anaemia
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A step‑by‑step clinical framework for evaluating anaemia in low‑resource settings, focusing on bedside assessment, likely tropical causes, and pragmatic investigations.

b: Hb <13 g/dL in men, <12 g/dL in non‑pregnant women, <11 g/dL in pregnant women.
Use peripheral smear to assess red cell size and morphology.
sections.p: Anaemia is a reduction in haemoglobin concentration below age‑ and sex‑specific normal ranges, confirmed by a full blood count (FBC).

b: Mild: Hb 10–12 g/dL (women) or 11–13 g/dL (men).
Moderate: Hb 8–9.9 g/dL.
Severe: Hb <8 g/dL; consider transfusion if symptomatic.
sections.p: Severity guides urgency of treatment and need for transfusion.

b: Nutritional deficiency – iron, folate, B12 (dietary scarcity, malaria‑related hemolysis).
Chronic infection – HIV, TB, malaria, schistosomiasis.
Hemolysis – sickle cell disease, G6PD deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis.
Blood loss – hookworm, uterine bleeding, gastrointestinal ulcer disease.
Bone‑marrow suppression – HIV, chemotherapy, aplastic anaemia.
sections.p: Classify by reduced production, increased loss, or increased destruction; think of common tropical and low‑resource conditions first.

b: Fatigue, dyspnoea on exertion, palpitations.
Pallor of conjunctivae, nail beds, palms.
Tachycardia, systolic flow murmur, widened pulse pressure.
In severe cases: chest pain, syncope, heart failure.
sections.p: Symptoms reflect tissue hypoxia; signs depend on chronicity and severity.
Prioritise tests that answer a specific clinical question; have alternatives when a test is unavailable.

t.a: Full blood count with red cell indices
t.b: Is the anaemia micro‑, normo‑ or macro‑cytic? Guides next step.
Is the marrow responding? High → hemolysis or blood loss; Low → production problem.
Is iron deficiency present? Low ferritin confirms deficiency.
Are macro‑cytic anaemias due to deficiency?
What morphological clues exist? Schistocytes, sickle cells, parasites.
Is hookworm or schistosomiasis causing chronic blood loss?

b: Hb <7 g/dL with cardiac disease or active bleeding.
Signs of heart failure or acute chest pain.
Severe dyspnoea, syncope, or altered mental status.
sections.p: Identify patients who need urgent intervention.

b: Sickle cell crisis – analgesia, hydration, treat infection; avoid NSAIDs if renal impairment.
Malaria‑related hemolysis – antimalarial therapy per national protocol; monitor for severe anaemia.
Severe anaemia – consider packed red cell transfusion if Hb <7 g/dL or symptomatic; cross‑match may be limited, use O‑negative if urgent.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive therapy.

b: Re‑check Hb 2–4 weeks after therapy.
Educate on iron‑rich diet, deworming, malaria prophylaxis, and safe childbirth practices.
Screen household contacts for hookworm or malaria in endemic regions.
sections.p: Ensure resolution of cause and prevent recurrence.

b: Chronic heart failure – may cause pallor and fatigue but has elevated JVP and peripheral oedema.
Hypothyroidism – can cause fatigue and macrocytosis but thyroid function tests differentiate.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic anaemia or share similar signs.
